J'ai conscience que Hitchcock est une référence dans les premiers films "psychologique" ( j'expliquerai le pourquoi des guillemets). Et, je pense qu'il est important de voir comment a l'époque il voyait les personnes psychiatrisées. Cependant, il faut arrêter de penser que cela reste une représentation intéressante. Au contraire c'est un film qui maintient les clichés psychophobe et dégradante. Étant une personne concernée je déteste Hitchcock pour ce que les gens en retienne. Un zhomme qui aurait soit disant réussi à créer des personnages à la psychologie complexe. (Pour l'époque peut être, mais plus du tout de nos jours.) Étant une référence que l'on ne remet jamais en question sur ce point, je trouve problématique que l'on normalise encore ces clichés dégradant et marginalisant.

“Here I was born, and there I died. It was only a moment for you; you took no notice.” As someone who has previously enjoyed each Hitchcock film I’ve been exposed too, I genuinely cannot bring myself to understand why this is so hyped. All the praise I see for this has to do with the symbolism and metaphors but can we talk about the actual narrative for a second? The plot here is one of the most contrived stories I’ve ever seen in a film, attempting to do way too much yet never taking the time to fully commit. Madeline is compelling for the first half but once the second half starts she doesn’t matter because the “character” isn’t real; Judy however is, but you don’t care to root for her because she’s an accomplice to murder and in love with the most mediocre man ever. Speaking of which: Scottie is such a boring main character. He’s a terrible PI who doesn’t get caught only because the person he’s following knows he’s there, he’s incredibly abusive to Judy prior him figuring out who she really is (No, grief is not an excuse), and ultimately he also just has an affair with whom he believes to be a married woman. My point is: none of the character are compelling or root-able by the end except for Midge, but the movie forgets about her even being a character following the second act. I get this is a very internal film from Hitchcock, but that doesn’t mean it’s a good movie. Yes the color, editing, and sound are great; but what I value most is narrative and this narrative is awfully paced with an abysmal payoff. I know this is going to go become one of my certified hot takes but I’ve gotta stand on business. Hitchcock is still on my Mount Rushmore of horror directors. But if you want to be an honest critic (even just for fun on Letterboxd), you gotta not just glaze everything a great director puts out. This wasn’t received well when it came out and I can see why. Is Hitchcock still a certified master? Yes. Do I still think this movie is kind of a narrative shitfest? Also yes.

I understand why this film is considered a classic and why it's popular but it's not for me. I found Alfred Hitchcock’s use of dolly zooms, slow and quiet scenes and color was a really unique and cool way of conveying confusion and the “vertigo effect”. Some scenes were put in a first person perspective of Scottie when he's experiencing acrophobia and there's a dolly zoom going downward. I thought this was really interesting because it lets the viewer experience this with him instead of just watching, I thought this fit really well with the whole disorienting and spiraling themes of the movie. Another thing Hitchcock did in Vertigo that was impressive to me was his use of color. When Scottie first spots Madeleine in the restaurant, she's wearing bright green and the background is a really bright red/pink, It's all so vibrant and surreal so I thought again this really fits that whole confusing vibe of everything But, nevermind how pretty the shots were, the coloring and cinematography just wasn't enough to keep me fully engaged with this film. I jumped at the opportunity to see a Hitchcock that I'd never seen before at one of my local cinemas. I love 'Rope' and 'Rear Window', so hearing that 'Vertigo' is one of Hitchcock's masterpieces seemed like a no-brainer. To discover that it's actually one of most overrated films ever made was a bit upsetting to say the least. We all left the cinema with a sour taste in our mouths, wishing we could get out $16 back and that someone had told us the truth: 'Vertigo' actually kind of sucks. Hitchcock: the master of suspense. Little to no suspense in the whole film. What makes many of his other films great is that we as the audience know things that the characters don't. Never the case here. The pacing? Painfully slow and borderline unengaging. The twist was apparent from halfway through the film, so the second half was just enduring one sad and tiresome display of misogyny after another. How Jimmy Stewart became such a popular heart-throb in the 40s-60s is beyond me. He just mostly plays unlikable assholes that somehow women still like. Plenty of people seem to say how gorgeous this film looks as well. The depiction of San Francisco, the bright colours, and the one major dream sequence stand out of bold and expressive. Yet, so much of the film is also filmed in bland locations, with uninspired set-pieces and straight-forward blocking. I wasn't nearly as impressed as I expected to be. Then, to wrap everything up. The ending is terrible, with no sense of mystery or closure to hold onto, just a sad dead-end with no real enjoyment or satisfaction. The entire second half is a painful ordeal. It's hard to believe I watched the same film that hundreds of thousands of men and women over the last 58 years have given 8/10, 9/10, or 10/10 reviews to, or called Hitchcock's masterpiece. A predictable, slow, stale, offensive and mostly just off-putting drag. Sad. 4/10

The first thing I liked that Hitchcock did was add a point of view to the film. When watching and seeing from Scottie's point of view, it helps you have a better understanding of the movie. We see this constantly when Scottie is driving and is following Madeline through San Francisco. From this, you can see Scottie, but you also get to see where he is going and how he is constantly following her. The point-of-view shot was used multiple times in the film, and another time is when he is running up the stairs at the church trying to save Madeline. In this scene, the point-of-view shot shows Scottie's acrophobia and how it is preventing him from saving the love of his life. To add on, in this scene, the dolly zoom was used to emphasize his fear and add suspense to the film to see if he will be able to save her. The dolly zoom was used twice, and both times it was to show his fear. In my opinion, the first dolly zoom was foreshadowing because his fear led to someone dying, and then later in the film that happened again when he was running up the church; even though fake Madeline didn’t die, Scottie thought she did. I also think that color in this film was very important and adds to Scottie's obsession because when we see Scottie, there is usually something red around him; for example, we once saw Scottie wearing a red suit, and red reflects danger and evil, and at the end of the movie Scotties obssesion caused him to become evil towards judy especaillywhen he made her wear the certian clothes. In my opinion, the “Cardinal Sins of Cinema” I struggled with the most in this movie was it being too slow. It's weird because there were times when I felt that some scenes were too long and some were too short. Times when I thought it was too long were when Scottie was driving and following Madeline, for example when they were driving into the woods and the bay; I felt that they could have been just a little shorter. I also wish that the ending scene was longer because I feel that the ending was abrupt. She fell through the window, then it just ended. In my opinion, I prefer when movie endings wrap up the story more and not leave it up for interpretation. Some people may think this movie is too old, but I honestly don't think so because I know if I had watched this in 1958, I would have been gagged by the plot twist. The coloring of this film also adds another element to it that makes it a classic. I feel like I didn’t enjoy it as much because I am used to watching movies now with better action and more complex plot twists. Overall, though, I feel this still can be considered a movie classic even though I would never rewatch it again.

Vertigo interests me as a foundation for the future of films. While I did enjoy it, I consider this film GOOD, but not GREAT. It's narrative is interesting, and honestly clearly well thought out, but not perfectly executed. I loved the reveal of the mystery, but hated how it was revealed to the audience, while still having an hour of the film left. I like the theory that Scottie has ling before figured it out, and is testing Judy, but so little evidemce is given to support that, that i'm not sure if i'm just reaching. Hitchcock makes very bold creative decisions, especially for 1958 under classic cinemas systems. I love how he blends animation with live action footage for the nightmare sequence, adding psychedelic imagery to an audience who obviously hated it, as well as LOVING his use of colour on set and costume to subtly showcase themes of greed, love, and obsession to the point of destruction. It's really fun to look back on certain moments with that in mind. However the negatives really out weigh my opinion of the film, like how Scottie's vertigo really is underused, and the ending of this film is genuinely the worst film ending I've ever seen, it felt like they got to the end of the script snd just said fuck it, idk what to do 😭. Hitchcock's vision, and directing is impressive, but not that well excecuted. Overall with all the hype I expected A LOT better of a film. But still interesting to see a foundation for Hollywoods later creatives to have surely taking inspiration from! Coming out of Rear Window , my expectations for Hitchcock were that this would be a small, yet creatively-shot movie. Instead, it was massive, intricate, and impressive from all filmmaking standpoints—until its throwaway of an ending. Vertigo was a dark and complex story which keeps its audience on edge and guessing as there is never a moment where at least one of its characters isn’t going insane. It’s not a simple story with simple characters like Rear Window , and it definitely doesn’t leave anyone with a good feeling. The tricks that Hitchcock used to make some of the sequences magnificent are incredible to learn about, and the visuals—whether they be the stunning, colorfully-charged cinematography or the masterworks of 1950s editing that makes us feel uncomfortable yet fill us with wonder at the same time, this is a journey. The pure intention behind the focuses and the frames and even the shapes leave the viewer with a lot to dissect, until the ending discourages everything. This film was written incredibly well and its plot twist was a genuine shock. It felt like, through all its twists and turns, it was building up to a magnificent crescendo, but instead, its ending seemed to forget everything about the movie. Sure, it may seem like poetic justice, but that doesn’t change the fact that it didn’t make sense. Hitchcock impressed me with Vertigo, but I left frustrated as all the bells and whistles and hooks didn’t pay off in the end. For a journey of all sorts that never finds its destination, watch Vertigo. For a simple yet satisfying story, watch Rear Window .

I was very shocked by the way the film ended because I was not expecting the story to take the direction that it did. After Madeleine supposedly committed suicide, John became obsessed with her and was unable to move on. When Judy came into his life, he wanted to change everything about her so that she would resemble Madeleine. Eventually, John took Judy back to the bell tower where Madeleine had “died” , the reason why he took Judy there was because he wanted to relive what had happened and become the hero he was not able to be the first time. Judy was scared and upset about being there, but John was determined to make it to the top. Once they reached the top of the bell tower, Judy became startled when she saw a shadowy figure and backed away and ended up falling to her death. I think the way that this movie was created was beautiful. There were a lot of colors, lighting, and sound effects that really stood out to me. For instance, when Judy is done with her makeover to look like Madeleine, there is a part where she steps out of the powder room and the lighting changes. Judy looks sad at first, but then she starts to smile, while John looks at her almost like he is seeing the ghost of Madeleine. This scene stuck with me because the expressions of the characters, lighting, and the sound effects, make everything seem eerie and unsettling. I think that this film is important to film studies because of the cinematography, along with the psychological effects that it produces. For instance, the obsession that John has with trying to make Judy more like Madeleine is quite alarming and can make for an interesting topic in studies.

Vertigo mi lascia in una posizione strana: lo trovo molto più interessante da pensare che da guardare. L’ho visto in più riprese, e anche nei tratti seguiti tutti d’un fiato mi sono annoiato spesso. Buona parte di questa distanza dipende dal mio rapporto generale con la Hollywood classica: la patina elegante, la fotografia levigata, la musica orchestrale che costruisce mondi quasi onirici – tutto questo mi fa spesso scivolare in una sorta di torpore, anche quando il film, sotto, racconta cose forti. Vertigo non fa eccezione, e per questo non sono riuscito a entrarci emotivamente. Ma è proprio da lì che parte quello che mi sembra il cuore del film: Hitchcock non abbandona mai il linguaggio hollywoodiano, lo usa fino in fondo e poi lo fa esplodere dall’interno con le sue stesse regole. Prima costruisce il sogno – la donna misteriosa, bellissima, irraggiungibile, la fotografia da favola, la musica romantica – e ci lascia cadere anche noi, insieme a Scottie, dentro quell’idealizzazione. Poi ci mostra il dietro le quinte: Scottie che sceglie il vestito di Judy, il trucco, il colore dei capelli, l’acconciatura, come un regista che modella la propria attrice. È lo stesso meccanismo che il cinema classico applica alla diva, messo a nudo e reso quasi morboso. Per questo Vertigo mi sembra parlare più di desiderio che di amore. Scottie non ama Madeleine come persona: la Madeleine che conosce non esiste, è un’immagine costruita da Elster su una donna reale, e poi ricostruita di nuovo nella testa di Scottie. Midge invece esiste davvero, è disponibile, potrebbe stargli vicino senza ostacoli – e infatti non la desidera, o non allo stesso modo. Madeleine lo attrae proprio perché resta sempre fuori portata: il desiderio qui si nutre di distanza, non di vicinanza. Judy è vittima di tutto questo, ma è anche prigioniera della propria scelta di restare. Accetta di farsi ricostruire pezzo per pezzo perché ama Scottie, sapendo che lui sta amando qualcun’altra attraverso di lei. La scena che mi è rimasta più impressa è quella della stanza d’hotel, con Judy avvolta nella luce verde: in quel momento la donna reale sembra sparire dietro l’immagine desiderata, e non è solo Scottie a ricostruirla – è Hitchcock stesso, con luce, colore e Kim Novak, a farlo davanti a noi. Per questo il rischio di desiderare quell’immagine artificiale non riguarda solo il personaggio, ma anche lo spettatore. Quando più avanti Scottie vede la collana e capisce tutto, non scopre solo di essere stato ingannato: scopre che la Madeleine che aveva amato non è mai esistita in quel modo. La perde due volte. Il titolo italiano mi ha fatto pensare a questo: Judy viene costruita due volte come Madeleine, prima da Elster per ingannare Scottie, poi da Scottie stesso per riportare in vita quello che pensava di aver perso. E la vertigine del titolo, per me, non è solo l’altezza. Ce ne sono almeno tre: quella fisica di Scottie, quella percettiva – non riesce più a distinguere Judy da Madeleine, il reale dal costruito – e quella del desiderio, che continua a inseguire qualcosa che proprio perché idealizzato non si può raggiungere davvero. Nel finale Scottie supera la paura dell’altezza salendo sulla torre, ma nello stesso momento sprofonda nell’altra vertigine, quella psicologica. Guarisce da una e viene divorato dall’altra. Anche la struttura del film sembra girare su sé stessa più che procedere in avanti: si apre con Scottie davanti a un vuoto e si chiude allo stesso modo. Non credo che Hitchcock voglia semplicemente condannare Scottie per aver idealizzato una donna: mi sembra che gli interessi soprattutto mettere in scena come funziona l’idealizzazione – da dove nasce, perché seduce, come deforma lo sguardo sull’altro, e cosa succede quando pretendiamo che una persona reale coincida con quello che ci siamo costruiti in testa. La realtà, in Vertigo, semplicemente non rispetta l’immagine che ne abbiamo fatto, e Scottie passa il film a cercare di costringerla a farlo. Resta però la mia contraddizione di partenza: tutto questo lo trovo affascinante da analizzare, ma guardare il film mi ha annoiato. Ammiro Vertigo più di quanto mi sia piaciuto viverlo, ed è proprio questa distanza a giustificare il mio ★★★½: abbastanza per riconoscere quanto sia intelligente e stratificato, non abbastanza per fingere un coinvolgimento che, per me, semplicemente non c’è stato.

Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo reminds us that a movie, no matter the age, with a compelling story, engaging characters, and a genius use of visual techniques can create an entertaining cinematic experience. This movie shines in all these categories and, personally, has made this film a personal favorite of mine.  The first aspect of the film I really enjoyed was the emphasis on color as meaning. Hitchcock was a master at showing and not telling with a film, and this movie really proves that. The film’s Technicolor made Hitchcock’s storytelling through color really shine. You can tell when the film intends to invoke a certain idea or emotion, such as Madeleine’s silhouette shots with the green neon lights from the hotel sign illuminating the space. It seemed as though green invoked a sense of mystery to Madeleine’s character as Scottie slowly began to unravel the truth behind her aura. The color red also comes into play as it helps emphasize Scottie’s slow turn to obsession and lust for Madeleine’s image. The ultra-vibrant Red restaurant, a strong example of this technique, started to appear more frequently as Scottie began to spiral into psychological obsession. Another technique I really appreciated was the film’s pacing. Vertigo highlighted the importance of setting the plot with a slow start, and using that slow pace to parallel a sense of mystery and suspense. This film didn’t feed action in every scene; it kept the audience intrigued by creating a compelling case. The compelling Madeline case made me pay attention to the film even more, and as I realized, it surely rewarded me in the end with the movie’s signature twist. Pacing is really important because the more you pay attention, the more the film rewards you. To be honest, Vertigo did not challenge me in any of its aspects. Honestly, it was really refreshing watching a film that was slow and long because it helped me feel more connected to the story. This film did not feel forced or rushed; the unique story felt authentic to human experience. The psychological aspect of the film felt real because obsession, no matter what it can be about, could be experienced by anyone. With the success of the movie Obsession in 2026, I can see some similarities between both. Now, this doesn’t mean Vertigo Is the 1950s version of Obsession, but I can see some parallels between Bear’s character and Scottie's character. Both characters form a perfect image of their women, and with this obsession, slowly evolve from innocent loveable characters, to serious toxic individuals. After watching Obsession, I do have a better understanding of Vertigo. Watching Obsession helped me understand Scottie’s character on a much deeper level, especially because of the parallels with Bear. I could somehow know what Scottie was feeling and how his obsession would cause harm to his life after recalling what Bear went through in Obsession. In conclusion, Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo deserves to be recognized as a true classic. Its compelling, suspenseful, and rewarding story stands out among many modern films.

Meditando tra me e me, ho avvertito quasi il dovere di fissare qui e ora una testimonianza su Vertigo, un’opera con cui Alfred Hitchcock ha consegnato al cinema una forma di maestria assoluta – seppur sia lecito e possibile misurarsi con la statuaria marmoreità di una simile pellicola.  Occorre innanzitutto collocare il film nella sua giusta luce contestuale, a partire dalle rivoluzioni formali che ha saputo innestare nell’esperienza della visione. Come non concedere a Hitchcock la paternità di quell’effetto vertiginoso – una prodigiosa innovazione visiva per l’epoca –, che è soltanto la prima di un’infinita serie di scarti tecnici e concettuali impressi all’impianto cinematografico? Ma vi è un momento specifico che tocca una delle mie personali fragilità artistiche, un punto in cui pittura, cinema e letteratura sembrano fondersi: la sequenza onirica disegnata dal pittore John Ferren, impregnata delle suggestioni dell’espressionismo astratto. In quell’intervallo così breve, eppure così denso, il film riesce a mostrare ciò che quasi mai al cinema è dato scorgere con pari evidenza: l’architettura interna della mente, la res cogitans pulsante e tormentata del protagonista, Scottie.  Eppure, a questo punto vorrei scostare le consuete partizioni del discorso critico per concedere alla riflessione un respiro più genuinamente filosofico. «L’arte imitativa è quindi lungi dal vero, e per questo, a quanto sembra, modella ogni cosa: perché tocca solo una piccola parte di ciascuna, e questa non è che un simulacro», scriveva Platone. Vi è un’impronta schiettamente platonica nella celebre sequenza della signora Valdés, dove solo in seguito Scottie scoprirà che la donna non ha mai abitato davvero i luoghi in cui pure appariva presente. Nel corso di tutta la visione, un interrogativo continua a ritornare, tenace e insidioso: che cosa vi è di autenticamente reale all’interno di questo film?  In nostro soccorso giunge Jean Baudrillard: «Fascinazione per la norma massima e la maestria delle probabilità. Vertigine del modello, che si unisce al modello della morte... Basta guardarlo per avere la vertigine. La vertigine di un mondo senza difetti». Madeleine Elster – o la signora Valdés, che dir si voglia – incarna alla perfezione questo concetto: è il simulacro puro, compiuto, assoluto.  Infine, non si può tacere della travolgente bellezza dei corpi e delle forme. Tutto in questo film obbedisce a un’estetica esasperata, che confina perennemente con un’estasi che oserei definire afrodisiaca, richiamando quasi la presenza del divino. Dalla presenza fisica degli attori ai loro volti, fino alla misura impeccabile delle loro recitazioni: ogni singolo elemento converge e si ricompone all'interno di una sublime, vertiginosa estetica della bellezza.

Today was my 30th birthday! I took my parents out to lunch and then brought them back to my place. We were going to head out to an IMAX re-release of The Shining, but my mother didn't like the trailer, which is just the scene where a river of blood sloshes out of the elevator. My father was also unenthusiastic about my pitch for the film - "It's about the white man's murder of the Native Americans!". I also had some mild reservations about rewatching a movie I'd just watched 6 months prior. The whole point of this hobby is to broaden my horizons after all. So we decided to stay in and watch a film on my new 65" TV. I presented two alternatives - Vertigo and Goldfinger. The moment I mentioned Alfred Hitchcock and the San Francisco setting (we're in the Bay Area), my mother was sold on Vertigo. I was also excited to watch what I've regularly seen ranked as the best film ever made (alongside Citizen Kane). By coincidence, I'd just seen Vertigo star James Stewart in a holiday screening of It's a Wonderful Life, and here I got to see him go from the charismatic leader he was there to a broken, twisted man driven mad by a combination of his vertigo (phobia of heights) and trauma over his apparent love interest (the wife of a man who hired him as a private eye) committing suicide in front of him. When he finds a woman a year later who looks exactly like his lover, the mystery around his lover's suicide starts to unravel and the viewer gets disoriented so badly from the revelation that we truly understand the sensation of "vertigo" ourselves. My mother was excitedly pointing out various landmarks she recognized ("That's the presidio! That's Sausalito!") as the film progressed, and we resolved to visit more of the Bay Area together. To my and my father's amazement, she also predicted various plot points before they transpired ("She's not dead! It's a dummy!", "The necklace! He'll know it's her from the necklace!"). Philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer observed that a man inherits his intellect from his mother, and I see the truth of that. After we finished watching the movie and my parents left, I re-read Roger Ebert's essay describing the film in his Great Movies and finally had the context to appreciate it. I close with a quote from it. "As Scottie embraces “Madeleine,” even the background changes to reflect his subjective memories instead of the real room he’s in. Bernard Herrmann’s score creates a haunting, unsettled yearning. And the camera circles them hopelessly, like the pinwheel images in Scottie’s nightmares, until the shot is about the dizzying futility of our human desires, the impossibility of forcing life to make us happy. This shot, in its psychological, artistic, and technical complexity, may be the one time in his entire career that Alfred Hitchcock completely revealed himself, in all of his passion and sadness. (Is it a coincidence that the woman is named Madeleine—the word for the French biscuit which, in Proust, brings childhood memories of loss and longing flooding back?) Alfred Hitchcock took universal emotions, like fear, guilt, and lust, placed them in ordinary characters, and developed them in images more than in words. His most frequent character, an innocent man wrongly accused, inspired much deeper identification than the superficial superman in today’s action movies."

Vertigo starts on a close-up of an eye before the title spirals out of it, and that single image tells you everything about what Alfred Hitchcock is about to do to you: pull you into someone else's obsessive, spiraling point of view and never quite let you out. The cold open is genuinely anxiety-inducing — a cop falls to his death, Scottie left dangling from the gutter, powerless — and then, with almost no transition, the tone flips entirely into a colorful, mannered art-gallery scene, a woman studying a painting, a man trying to balance a walking stick like nothing traumatic just happened. Hitchcock, a director who spent his career finding the dread hiding inside polite society, has rarely made the whiplash between horror and elegance this explicit. That gallery sequence is the film's real hinge. The painting itself is gorgeous, and the way Madeline's bouquet and hair seem lifted directly out of it is the first sign that this woman may not be entirely her own person. The receptionist casually mentioning she hadn't seen Carlotta come in that day is a small line that quietly detonates the whole plot — once Carlotta and Madeline are connected, the story stops being a simple tail job and becomes something much stranger. And there's a real ache underneath all of it: those postcard-perfect San Francisco landscapes, the Golden Gate Bridge shot with Madeline and Scottie beneath it, carry a wistfulness for an era that already felt like a memory even in 1958 — the kind of beauty that makes you yearn for a past you never actually lived through. Scottie fighting his acrophobia to save Madeline only for it to mean nothing later is the film's cruelest joke, and once Gavin's scheme is revealed — that he was the one who threw the real body, that Madeline was alive and complicit the whole time — the earlier romance curdles into something much sicker in hindsight. Which makes the back half almost unbearable to watch: Scottie seeing Madeline in every woman he passes, the woman who bought his car, the one across the restaurant, and finally trying to physically remake Judy into Madeline, right down to hunting for the same grey suit. It's a sick, obsessive kind of love story, and yet Hitchcock stages it with such aching sincerity that you can't help but feel for Scottie anyway, even as you watch him try to resurrect a woman who was a performance all along.

Now I understand "High Anxiety". I thought "Vertigo" would be challenging to my media literacy. Challenging to sit through, yes, but it's worth it. Although I don't cover much Hitchcock, I can safely say this was his magnum opus and I saw "Psycho". An ultimate slowburn, your senses are positively shattered as you witness remarkable cinematography (that Golden Gate Bridge shot made me cream myself); innovative technologies notably the first usage of the dolly zoom; languid dreamy pacing; and breathtaking performances from Stewart and Novak in dual roles. Oh-so-slowly, you watch characters go from likable to hardly sympathetic towards the conclusion and you question yourself too. This features the *BEST* examination of obsession, illusion, and madness and while you can't excuse their behavior, you just feel sorry for almost everybody involved. The progression from mystery thriller to an almost character study on Madeleine and John is masterful. What's this movie without discussing its color coding? Green's prominent; you usually think of nature or nausea (makes narrative sense with acrophobia), but it also represents the fantastic; danger, and love. There's a pinch of paranormal with mentions of possession and doppelgangers, Novak even looks like a spirit in one scene. Bernard Herrmann conducted a mystifying score which swirls and messes with your mind. I wanna talk about John for a second: his mental transformation during act three is eerie and heartbreaking. Like I said, you ruminate about his psyche and it explains everything yet doesn't excuse it. Hitchcock knew how to create flawed, interesting characters and moody tension. And you want an abrupt ending? *THIS* might be the most abrupt! Smart, terrifying, and nightmarishly gorgeous, "Vertigo" will make you dizzy from its visuals, themes, and characters.

Rewatching a classic Hitchcock on 35mm at the Art Theatre in Long Beach with my husband was a mesmerizing experience. Vertigo was clearly ahead of its time, with its vast dreamlike scenes and its unconventional structure. It definitely feels like an influence on David Lynch, who we know was a big fan. I love the colors, the acting, the Bernard Herrmann score, the cinematography by Robert Burks (of many of Hitch’s other films such as Rear Window and The Birds), and every other aspect of this cinema perfection. On this second watch, I appreciated Kim Novak’s performance even more. Her ability to play two distinctly different people is pretty astounding. And of course James Stewart and Barbara Bel Geddes are stunning in this. Like Thelma Ritter in Rear Window, Bel Geddes is yet another supporting performance in another Hitchcock film that steals the show whenever it’s featured on the screen. AFI Silver. Hitchcock/Hermann. 70mm. Everyone loves a Hitchcock film, but a Hitchcock/Hermann film? Amazing. AFI did a series of all eight films that featured the historic collaboration between director Alfred Hitchcock and musician Bernard Herrmann. Per AFI: "Hitchcock and Hermann collaborated on eight films over an 11-year period. Despite their differing backgrounds and opposite temperaments, "Benny and Hitch" formed a close working relationship, resulting in some of their most beloved and enduring works." I was able to see seven out of the eight films at AFI Silver! This was the third film I saw at AFI. This is one of my favorite films of all time, full stop. It's hard to describe just how brilliant this film is in every way, and that includes the score. As AFI states, this is "Alfred Hitchcock's supreme achievement, the fullest expression of his cinematic obsessions and the one that goes the furthest in pursuit of them." It's hard to overstate how good this film is. And seeing it on 70mm was of course a real treat.
